blocks.md: **Naive pattern search = O(n·m) rescan. KMP pays O(m) preprocessing so the TEXT POINTER NEVER MOVES BACKWARD.**

The engine is the **failure table lps[i]** = length of longest proper prefix of pattern that is also suffix ending at i. Mismatch after matching k chars? Fall back to lps[k−1], not to start — already-matched context survives partially.

items.title: Find the Index of First Occurrence (strStr) — KMP required
items.statement: Implement lps build + search loop; then defend Θ(n+m) with pointer-monotonicity.
hints: Section trace doubles as your test.

solutionCode.label: KMP: longest-proper-prefix-suffix table, then a non-backtracking scan

items.complexity: Theta(n + m) — building the LPS table is O(m), the scan is O(n), and neither pointer ever moves backwards. Space O(m).

followups.q: Defend Theta(n + m) despite the inner fallback.
followups.a: The text pointer i never decreases. The pattern pointer j increases by one per match and only decreases on a fallback — and since j rises at most n times total, it can fall at most n times total. So the fallbacks are amortised across the whole scan, giving O(n) rather than O(nm). That monotonicity is the entire argument.

followups.q: Why fall back to lps[len-1] instead of resetting len to 0?
followups.a: Resetting throws away a real partial match. On pattern "aab" scanning "aaab", after mismatching you still have "a" matched — lps tells you exactly how much prefix survives. Resetting to 0 is what turns KMP back into the naive algorithm while looking correct on simple inputs.

items.title: Find All Anagrams in a String

solutionCode.label: delta counter plus a "how many letters are still wrong" scalar

items.complexity: Time O(n) — one window pass, O(1) work per step via a running delta counter. Space O(1) (26 slots).

followups.q: Why a scalar counter rather than comparing two 26-arrays?
followups.a: Array comparison is 26 operations per window, so O(26n). The scalar tracks how many letters are currently unbalanced and updates in O(1) per character entering or leaving. It is the difference between a constant factor of 26 and a constant factor of 2 — same complexity class, very different in practice.

Windows at 0 ("ab"), 1 ("ba"), 2 ("ab") all balance, so the answer is [0,1,2]. Overlapping hits are the case a naive "find, then skip past the match" loop gets wrong — the window must slide by one, never by len(p).

items.title: Permutation in String
items.statement: Same machinery returning boolean at first zero-delta.

solutionCode.label: identical window, returns true at the first zero delta

items.complexity: Time O(n), space O(1). Same machinery as T302 with an early return.

followups.q: Why is the argument order (p, s) rather than (s, p)?
followups.a: LeetCode 567 signs it as checkInclusion(s1, s2) where s1 is the pattern. Getting it backwards silently searches the wrong direction and passes on symmetric inputs. Read the signature before assuming the conventional (haystack, needle) order.

followups.q: What is the only difference from Find All Anagrams?
followups.a: The return type and one line: instead of recording every match position, it returns true at the first. That is worth noticing out loud — the interviewer is checking whether you recognise a solved problem or start over from scratch.

items.title: Reverse Words in a String (in-place)
items.statement: C++ in-place three-pass: trim/compact spaces → reverse whole → reverse each word.
hints: Explain why word-reversal AFTER global reversal preserves order.

solutionCode.label: squeeze spaces, reverse everything, then reverse each word back

items.complexity: Time O(n) across three passes. Space O(1) when operating on a mutable buffer.

followups.q: Why does reversing each word AFTER the global reversal restore the order?
followups.a: Reversing the whole buffer puts the last word first — the order you want — but every word is spelled backwards. Reversing a word twice returns it to the original spelling while leaving its new position untouched, because the second reversal is confined within the word. Order and spelling are independent operations on disjoint scopes.

followups.q: Why is pass 1 necessary before the reversals?
followups.a: Without it, "  a  b " reverses into " b  a  " and the word-boundary pass has to cope with runs of spaces and leading or trailing gaps. Normalising to exactly one space between words and none at the ends means pass 3 can split on a single space with no special cases.

items.title: Multiply Strings
items.statement: Grade-school multiplication in buffers; strip leading zeros at end.
hints: Skip '0' output when result empty except one zero.

solutionCode.label: grade-school grid, reversed indexing at i+j+1
solutionCode.py:
def multiply(a: str, b: str) -> str:
    if a == "0" or b == "0":
        return "0"                        # avoid a buffer of all zeros
    m, n = len(a), len(b)
    buf = [0] * (m + n)                   # product has at most m+n digits
    for i in range(m - 1, -1, -1):
        for j in range(n - 1, -1, -1):
            mul = (ord(a[i]) - 48) * (ord(b[j]) - 48)
            low, high = i + j + 1, i + j  # low holds units, high the carry
            total = mul + buf[low]
            buf[low] = total % 10
            buf[high] += total // 10      # carry accumulates, resolved later
    out = "".join(str(d) for d in buf).lstrip("0")
    return out if out else "0"

items.complexity: Time O(m*n) for operands of m and n digits. Space O(m+n) for the result buffer.

followups.q: Why does a[i]*b[j] land at index i+j+1?
followups.a: Digit i from the left of an m-digit number has place value 10^(m-1-i). Multiplying two such gives place value 10^(m+n-2-i-j), which in an (m+n)-length buffer indexed from the left is position i+j+1. The +1 is what leaves room for the final carry at index 0.

followups.q: Why can the carry be added to buf[high] without immediate normalisation?
followups.a: buf[high] can temporarily exceed 9, but it is itself processed later in the loop as a "low" position for a smaller i or j, where the mod/div step normalises it. The final leftmost digit never exceeds 9 because the product of an m-digit and n-digit number fits in m+n digits. Deferring the carry is what keeps the inner loop branch-free.

items.title: Integer to English Words
items.statement: Chunked scale recursion; handle 1000000 → "One Million" (no 'and', no double spaces).

solutionCode.label: recurse over three-digit chunks, one scale name each

items.complexity: Time O(number of digits). Space O(1) beyond the output.

followups.q: Why does 1,000,000 not become "One Million Thousand"?
followups.a: Because the chunk test skips empty groups. 1000000 splits into chunks 0, 0, 1 — the two zero chunks contribute nothing and never emit their scale word. Emitting the scale unconditionally is the bug that produces "One Million Thousand".

followups.q: Where do the double-space bugs come from?
followups.a: From appending " " + scale when the chunk is empty, or joining chunks with an unconditional space. Building each part complete-and-trimmed, then joining only when the accumulator is non-empty, means no trimming pass is ever needed. English also has no "and" here — "One Hundred Five", not "One Hundred and Five".

items.title: Minimum Window Substring (hard preview)
items.statement: Smallest window covering ALL target chars incl. duplicates — need/formed counters like anagrams but variable width.
hints: formed==required triggers left-shrink while still covered.
Full sliding-window doctrine lands Module 10 — taste it now.

solutionCode.label: need/formed counters with a variable-width window

items.complexity: Time O(n + m) — each character enters and leaves the window at most once. Space O(number of distinct chars in t).

followups.q: Why compare with == rather than >= when updating formed?
followups.a: formed counts distinct characters that are *exactly* satisfied. Using >= would increment on every extra copy, so formed could exceed required and the loop condition would misfire. Incrementing only at the crossing point — and decrementing only when dropping back below it — keeps formed an accurate count of satisfied characters.

followups.q: Why does duplicates in t not break this?
followups.a: need stores counts, not presence, so t = "AABC" requires two As. window[A] must reach 2 before A counts as formed. A set-based version silently accepts a window with one A — the single most common wrong answer to this problem.
